 Supporters, opponents of Proposition 43 make final push going into midterm election
 BY 
 Jas Kang 
 Los Angeles 
 PUBLISHED 12:11 PM PT Oct. 30, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 12:11 PM PDT Oct. 30, 2026 
 SHARE 
 LOS ANGELES — With Election Day coming up Nov. 3, voters across California have several propositions on the ballot, including Proposition 43.
 If the proposition is passed, it would change the threshold to pass local taxes initiated through citizens for specific purposes such as fire protection or funding for schools to require a two-thirds majority vote, rather than a simple majority above 50%.
 Supporters and opponents of Prop. 43 are making their final push with the midterms taking place next week. 
 Susan Shelley’s with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assocation and is hoping to see voters say yes to Prop. 43 because of the financial pressures that many California residents are facing. 
 “The cost of living is so high in California, and people are really hurting,” she said. “And then you go to the ballot, and you see the governments or these special interests saying, if you don’t vote for a tax increase, we won’t have a fire department.”
 Several local governments have voiced their opposition to Prop. 43, including the cities of Glendale and Long Beach, because they said it would make it difficult to fund emergency departments and other public needs. But Shelley said that financial mismanagement by municipal officials has contributed to the issues. 
 “Why isn’t the city budget prioritized to pay for the fire department?” she said. “Why does it take another sales tax?”
 Elen Asatryan is a City Council member in Glendale and said that with a push for more resources for local residents, like affordable housing, it’s important to keep the 50%, so a simple majority can vote on the needs of the community. 
 “We have a project that’s coming in at 682 units. That’s just one project,” Asatryan said. "That is going to bring in thousands of new people into my city. Who’s paying for dispatch? How am I making sure that I still have the number of firefighters that I need?"
 With some policy changes being made at the state level in recent years, Asatryan said local governments have been impacted. 
 “It keeps ripping off the power that local governments have,” she said. “And that local neighborhoods have on deciding on what they want for their own city.”
